abstract: |
  Value-added taxes (VAT) allow firms to deduct the taxes paid on purchases from the taxes collected on sales, creating an incentive for firms to overreport their purchases of inputs to reduce their tax bill. The fundamental issue in identifying input overreporting stems from two unobservables, true inputs and productivity. Because firms differ in productivity, a firm reporting high input use for a given level of output may be overreporting or less productive. I use a structural production-function approach and a subset of firms that share the same technology as the rest but report truthfully. I then use the common technology to predict how potentially tax-evading firms would behave without overreporting, and compare the prediction to what they report. My method requires only firm-level input and output data, and a truth-reporting group. The method thus applies equally to standard firm-level surveys, administrative data, or confidential tax records. I apply the method to a Colombian manufacturing survey from 1981 to 1991. During this period, the Colombian sales tax worked as a VAT and, due to government and market scrutiny, corporations refrained from overreporting inputs.
  
  The approach yields a simple statistical test to detect input overreporting. Under the null hypothesis of no overreporting, the test is robust to a wide family of specifications of the probability of detection and the cost of overreporting. Among the 5 largest industries, the test detects overreporting in all 4 industries subject to the sales tax, and, as expected, fails to reject in the industry exempt from it. In the median of the 7 largest industries where overreporting is detected, firms report inputs that are 16 percent larger, on average, than true inputs. Next, I show that failing to correct for overreporting yields output elasticities of materials that are larger, and productivity distributions that are more dispersed and less persistent. I then estimate a structural model of firm tax evasion to study how claimed deductions, and thus government tax revenue, respond to a counterfactual tax rate. I find that a 0.5 percent increase in the sales-tax rate raises claimed deductions by 16 to 28 percent.
  
  Finally, I exploit a sales-tax increase introduced by the 1983 reform to investigate how firms' overreporting responds to changes in the tax rate. I find that between 1983 and 1987, among the industries subject to the tax change, the ratio of overreported to true inputs rose by about 9 percentage points.
